sections.heading: Start with a service, not a shopping list
sections.body: A security executive needs to explain why a safeguard deserves time and money. Begin with the service the organisation must deliver. In this lesson, Alder Supply is a fictional distributor that accepts orders and sends stock to customers. Its order records, stock database, warehouse terminals and staff knowledge are assets because they support that service. The service owner understands the consequence of an interruption; a technical owner understands the components. Neither perspective is enough alone. Ask who uses the service, what decisions its information supports, what happens when it fails and which dependencies could stop it. This produces a useful scope before anyone counts vulnerabilities. All facts and numbers in this pilot are invented for practice.

sections.heading: obj-w1-1 · Classify a statement before choosing a response
sections.body:
Use five categories to keep cause and consequence distinct. An asset is something of value to the service. A threat is a circumstance or event with potential to cause harm, such as a malicious actor sending deceptive messages or a power failure. A vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited or triggered, such as excessive export permission or an untested power dependency. A control is a safeguard intended to change likelihood or consequence. Business impact is the resulting harm: delayed shipments, wrong invoices or lost customer confidence. A threat is not necessarily an attacker, and an asset can be information, a person, a process or a dependency rather than only equipment.

Now ask which security goal is harmed. Confidentiality concerns inappropriate disclosure: a customer list sent to an unauthorised recipient. Integrity concerns improper alteration: bank details changed without approval. Availability concerns whether authorised users can obtain a usable service when needed: the warehouse cannot retrieve an order. A single event may affect all three. Corrupted order data may be present and readable while unusable for dispatch, so uptime alone misses the business problem. Classify the statement as written; do not invent facts to force exactly one goal where several are plausible.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w1-1 · Six statements in context
sections.body: The COO gives six statements. (1) The order database is an asset. (2) A criminal sending a false invoice is a threat event. (3) A payment clerk may both alter and approve bank details: that is a vulnerability in separation of duties. (4) Independent approval of bank-detail changes is a control. (5) A forged account number replacing the correct one is an integrity loss; the unauthorised payment is a business impact. (6) The dispatch service is unreachable during the shipping window: this is an availability loss with delayed shipments as the consequence. Statement 5 contains two levels of description, so annotate both rather than calling every bad outcome a vulnerability. In a board discussion, this distinction prevents a response team from buying a tool for a symptom while leaving the approval weakness untouched.

sections.heading: obj-w1-2 · Build a chain that can support a decision
sections.body:
Write the chain as service → asset → threat → vulnerability → consequence → control. State a plausible mechanism between each pair. A risk chain is stronger when it explains how harm would occur, rather than merely placing nouns beside arrows. A control should interrupt that mechanism, reduce harm or improve detection/recovery. Name who can make it operate and what evidence would show it did. Ask what still goes wrong if the control works exactly as designed: that is a route to discussing residual exposure.

Do not convert uncertainty into invented precision. If no loss history or likelihood data exists, say that the exposure is plausible and identify the next evidence to collect. Compare options by the business outcome they change, their cost and their limitations. Avoiding a risky service, reducing exposure, sharing some financial consequences and consciously retaining residual risk are different decisions; a security analyst should present the choice to the accountable business owner. Insurance, for example, does not restore an unavailable order system or make an unsafe process safe.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w1-2 · Two chains and an executive choice
sections.body:
Chain A: dispatch depends on order records; a criminal obtains an overprivileged clerk session; bulk export permission lets the session extract all customer addresses; disclosure harms customer confidence. The application owner removes unnecessary export permission and reviews exceptional exports. This reduces bulk exposure, but permitted users can still disclose individual records. Evidence: test an ordinary clerk account and review a synthetic export log.

Chain B: dispatch depends on the inventory database; an operator makes a mistaken bulk update; unrestricted production write permission changes quantities; incorrect picks delay shipments. The operations owner requires a second approval for bulk changes and tests rollback on a copy. This can catch some errors, but collusion or an untested rollback remains possible. Evidence: a sample approval record and a timed rollback exercise.

The COO chooses to pilot the bulk-change control first because a stock reconciliation already revealed frequent mistakes, while asking for export-volume evidence before sizing the disclosure work. This is an explicit decision under limited evidence, not a claim that availability always outranks confidentiality. Record the assumptions, owner, next check and date to revisit.

sections.heading: Why identity is an operating model
sections.body: Alder Supply has added a sales team and an outsourced support engineer. Its CFO asks for MFA everywhere after a suspicious sign-in. That is a useful prompt to examine access, but identity security spans more than the sign-in screen. Someone decides which identities exist, who owns them, what they may do, how changes reach applications and how access ends. Identity and access management (IAM) coordinates these decisions. Draw the actual path from a business request to an enforced permission; an approved ticket that never changes the application is a broken control. Begin with the business service and risk chains from week 1 so that privilege follows a need rather than seniority.

sections.heading: obj-w2-1 · Separate authentication from authorization through the lifecycle
sections.body:
Authentication checks whether a claimant controls an authenticator bound to an account; it does not establish that the account should still exist or may read a particular record. Authorization evaluates permission for an action on a resource, usually with role and context. An authenticated sales user may read assigned customers while being denied payroll. Authentication and authorization may occur in different components, and the application must enforce its own data/action rules even when a central identity provider performs sign-in.

A joiner needs a reliable employment or contract trigger, a manager-approved role and application provisioning with a recorded owner. A mover needs a comparison of old and new duties: remove obsolete access as well as adding the new role. A leaver needs timely account disablement, downstream account removal and treatment of sessions, tokens and shared secrets where applicable. Human resources provides relationship changes; managers and data/service owners approve business need; IAM operators execute provisioning; application owners verify enforcement. Use reconciliation to compare expected and actual accounts, because manual apps and failed connectors can escape the central process. Reviews should test samples and exceptions, not just count closed tickets.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w2-1 · Joiner, mover and leaver
sections.body:
Mira joins sales. HR creates the relationship event, the sales manager approves assigned-customer access, IAM provisions her identity and the CRM owner tests that Mira can view her region but cannot export payroll. Her authenticator proves account control at sign-in; the CRM permission check determines which records she can access.

Mira moves to purchasing. The purchasing manager approves supplier access; the sales manager confirms the old sales duty has ended. IAM removes the old group and adds the new one. The CRM owner checks cached sessions and local roles instead of assuming the directory group is sufficient. When Mira leaves, HR sends the dated trigger, IAM disables login and revokes relevant sessions/tokens, and each application owner verifies removal. The procurement integration runs under a separate service identity, so it stays operational while any secrets Mira could access are reviewed. A sample denied login and denied API request provide better evidence than a ticket marked done.

sections.heading: obj-w2-2 · Match safeguards to three access paths
sections.body:
Multi-factor authentication uses distinct factor categories, such as possession of a device plus knowledge of a secret or a biometric activation factor. Two passwords are two secrets in the same category, not two factors. Methods also differ: a manually entered one-time code can be relayed to a genuine service by a phishing site, while appropriately implemented verifier-bound cryptographic authentication can resist that relay. Select methods with a recovery process, enrollment controls and usability in mind; an insecure help-desk reset can undermine a strong normal sign-in. This is conceptual guidance, not an assertion that an organisation conforms to a NIST assurance level.

A normal user needs constrained business permissions and appropriate authentication. An administrator additionally needs separation from routine browsing, limited privilege duration/scope, approval for sensitive changes, useful action logs and an emergency access process. Privileged access management (PAM) is the set of controls around powerful credentials and sessions; a vault alone cannot decide whether a database change is justified. A workload or service cannot rely on a human approving a push notification for each job. Prefer a supported workload identity or managed short-lived credential where feasible; otherwise tightly scope, protect, rotate and monitor secrets with an accountable owner. Human authentication guidance does not by itself specify machine identity design.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w2-2 · Three paths, three remaining risks
sections.body:
For sales staff, the application owner combines phishing-resistant sign-in where supported with assigned-customer permissions. Remaining risk: malware in a signed-in endpoint can misuse an active session. For the support engineer, the platform owner uses a separate administrator identity, time-limited approved elevation and reviewable administrative actions. Remaining risk: an approved administrator can still make a damaging change, so rollback and peer checks remain relevant. For the nightly stock integration, the integration owner uses a scoped workload identity allowed to update stock but unable to administer users. Remaining risk: compromise of the job runtime can misuse its allowed writes.

The CFO funds the administrator pilot first and requires a tested emergency account procedure before removing standing privilege. A controlled emergency exercise records who approved access, what changed and whether the temporary grant ended. The tradeoff is slower unplanned maintenance and a dependency on the identity service; the support team designs an exception process rather than leaving a universal bypass permanently open.

sections.heading: Architecture as an explanation of permitted work
sections.body: A security architecture diagram should let an executive ask a useful question: if this part fails or is compromised, what other work becomes possible? A cloud logo and a firewall icon cannot answer that. Start with a service request and show its route, the identities acting at each step and where an action is accepted or denied. An endpoint is the device or host where an action originates or runs. A network path carries traffic. An application interprets requests and decides business actions. These layers can each fail differently. A network connection to an API does not imply permission to change every record, and an application login does not prove the endpoint is healthy.

sections.heading: obj-w3-1 · Trace two flows through explicit boundaries
sections.body:
For each flow, write subject → endpoint/workload → entry point → application → data/dependency, then draw response and management paths where relevant. Label what travels, such as a request, token or record; distinguish human identity from workload identity. A trust boundary is a change in control or trust context, such as an unmanaged internet client entering a managed service, an employee device reaching an application, or an application accessing a database. At each boundary ask which component enforces the decision, what identity/context it sees and who owns its policy. Mark an unknown as unknown instead of filling it with a product logo.

Use basic network reasoning to check the sketch. Name resolution tells a client which address to reach; routing moves packets; a network rule may allow only a named source/destination/service; encrypted transport protects the channel when correctly configured. None alone authorizes a business transaction. Endpoints need maintained configurations, vulnerability handling and useful detection; a compromised device may send apparently legitimate requests. The purpose of this first diagram is to expose dependencies and policy gaps for a technical owner to validate, not to produce a deployable firewall configuration.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w3-1 · Customer order and warehouse update
sections.body:
Flow A: customer browser → public application gateway → order API → order database. The gateway owner permits the public web entry and rejects unwanted paths; the API owner authenticates a returning customer and checks ownership of the requested order; the database owner permits only the API workload identity to perform the necessary data actions. Internet-to-gateway, gateway-to-application and application-to-database are three boundaries with different owners and decisions. A public browsing feature may allow anonymous use; do not pretend every request needs the same identity.

Flow B: managed warehouse terminal → internal application entry → inventory API → stock database. The endpoint owner maintains device posture; the entry owner checks permitted device/user context; the API owner limits stock adjustment actions to authorised warehouse roles; the database owner scopes the API identity. Draw the response with stock status back to the terminal. The CIO notices both services depend on the same identity provider and asks how an outage affects dispatch. Showing that dependency is more useful than colouring everything inside the network green.

sections.heading: obj-w3-2 · Compare reachable paths, not labels
sections.body:
In a flat design, many devices can reach many internal services. After compromising one terminal, an attacker may discover administrative interfaces and try stolen credentials against unrelated systems. Segmentation restricts which communication paths can exist and can reduce this opportunity. It needs enforced rules, maintained inventories and tests: two different subnets with unrestricted routing do not establish useful isolation. In a segmented design, show both the blocked lateral path and the remaining allowed path; an attacker may still abuse a broadly privileged application account over a legitimate connection.

Zero Trust adds an explicit assumption: network location and enterprise ownership alone do not justify access to a resource. Identity, device/context evidence and policy inform resource-specific decisions; enforcement and monitoring make those decisions real. Segmentation can support that approach, but it is not the whole model and does not remove identity, application or endpoint responsibilities. Explain the policy decision component separately from the point that enforces the decision. Check how policy updates reach enforcement and what happens when identity or posture information is unavailable. A simplistic fail-open rule can restore work while exposing sensitive paths; a simplistic fail-closed rule can stop critical operations. An approved, bounded contingency path is an operational design decision.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w3-2 · A limited redesign with two controls
sections.body:
Flat baseline: a stolen terminal session can attempt connections to the backup console; a reused administrator credential may then permit backup deletion. Proposed control 1: the network owner restricts backup management access to a dedicated administration path and tests a denied connection from the terminal segment. Failure mode: a broad emergency rule silently restores reachability. Tradeoff: troubleshooting and new service onboarding take more planning.

Proposed control 2: the backup service owner requires a separate time-limited administrator grant and verifies the managed administration endpoint before accepting destructive actions where supported. Failure mode: a compromised approved administrator session still performs permitted harm. Tradeoff: urgent restoration may depend on the identity/elevation service. In the new design the terminal-to-console path is blocked, but the approved administrator-to-console path remains and must be monitored and recoverable.

The CIO approves a staged pilot: observe required flows, test synthetic business transactions and denied paths, then restrict one segment with a rollback plan. The team measures blocked legitimate work and reachable unwanted paths, not the number of appliances installed. This tests assumptions before expanding a design that might disrupt dispatch.

sections.heading: The decision is about usable information
sections.body: Alder Supply can keep a database encrypted and still lose a week of business if nobody can restore the key or reconstruct accepted orders. Data protection combines decisions about who may see or change information, where copies travel and how a usable service returns after failure. Begin by identifying a dataset and its business owner. Include active databases, exports, temporary files, logs and backup copies. A control assessment states what is protected, how the control works, what evidence supports it and what remains uncertain. It is not a list of encryption product names or a legal compliance declaration. This lesson uses fictional operational decisions and makes no Swiss or EU legal applicability claims.

sections.heading: obj-w4-1 · Turn classification into handling and cryptographic decisions
sections.body:
Classify information according to consequences, using labels defined by the organisation. For this exercise use public, internal and restricted. Explain why a customer delivery dataset is restricted, who approves access and which handling actions follow: limit bulk exports, protect approved transfers, restrict backup readers and define retention/disposal with the appropriate owner. A label without these rules changes nothing. Integrity and availability can be critical even for public data, such as published product safety instructions.

Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext that can be recovered with appropriate key material. At-rest protection addresses stored copies under a stated threat model; encrypted transport addresses data travelling between endpoints. Neither prevents an authorised application from producing plaintext for an allowed user, so permissions and endpoint controls still matter. Hashing produces a digest rather than recoverable ciphertext. Comparing a file digest to a trustworthy expected digest can reveal changes, but an attacker who replaces both the file and its untrusted digest can defeat that check. Authenticity needs a trusted reference or an appropriate authenticated construction; do not treat a bare hash as proof of who created a record.

Key management is an operating responsibility: who can use keys, who can change access, how loss/compromise is handled and how recovery works. Separate data ownership from technical key custody and test their coordination. Keys may be managed by a platform service, but the organisation still must understand permissions, recovery dependencies and supported lifecycle functions. This introductory assessment does not select algorithms, prescribe cryptoperiods or assert platform compliance.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w4-1 · A classified order export
sections.body:
The sales director requests an order export for a courier. The data owner classifies addresses as restricted for this fictional exercise and approves only records needed for delivery. The application owner limits the export role and uses an approved protected transfer endpoint; the storage owner protects the stored export and backup copies. The key-management owner controls decryption permissions and tests recovery of the required key material through the supported platform process.

The CFO asks whether an encrypted disk prevents a clerk from emailing the export. It does not: the signed-in application can decrypt permitted data. Restricting export scope and handling is a different control. A trusted digest can help detect accidental change during a controlled transfer, but publishing a digest beside a file on a compromised endpoint is not independent authenticity evidence. The assessment records residual risks of a misaddressed delivery and a compromised authorised account rather than declaring the dataset safe because encryption is enabled.

sections.heading: obj-w4-2 · Set recovery objectives before selecting backup mechanics
sections.body:
The recovery time objective (RTO) states the target duration to restore a defined system or service function after disruption. Define the clock and usable outcome so a team does not stop timing when a virtual machine boots while customers still cannot order. The recovery point objective (RPO) states how far back data recovery may go, commonly expressed as an acceptable interval of lost updates. It is a different dimension: restoring quickly from an old copy can meet time and fail data-loss expectations. Business owners set needs with technical feasibility and dependencies in view. Objectives are targets, not evidence of actual capability.

A backup job reports that a copy operation completed under its own checks. Recovery also depends on usable copies, keys, identity access, application configuration, capacity, people and a safe environment. Replication can reproduce corruption or deletion, so ask which independent recovery options survive the chosen failure. Plan a restore exercise on an isolated environment with synthetic or otherwise appropriately handled test data; state authorisation, stop conditions and production boundaries. Verify integrity and business behaviour after restoration, not just file counts. Keep a record of timings, recovered transaction point, failed steps, owners and follow-up actions. A single test supports a bounded claim for that scenario and version, not a promise that every disaster can be recovered.

sections.heading: Worked example for obj-w4-2 · A test that exposes a gap
sections.body:
The COO sets an illustrative RTO of four hours for accepting and dispatching orders and an RPO of one hour. For this exercise the clock begins at declared service disruption and ends after the business owner accepts a successful synthetic order-to-dispatch transaction. At 12:00 a simulated outage begins. The newest usable backup reflects 10:30. Technical restore finishes at 14:20; a missing key permission delays application checks until 15:00. The business owner accepts the synthetic transaction at 15:15. Elapsed recovery is three hours fifteen minutes, meeting the four-hour target for this test. The recovery point is ninety minutes old at disruption, missing the one-hour RPO. Fast restoration did not fix the data-loss gap.

The recovery lead captures both measurements and the key-permission delay. The database owner proposes more frequent recoverable points and tests the full restore chain, while the business owner checks whether missing orders can be reconciled safely. The next exercise repeats the failed assumption rather than reporting overall success from one green backup dashboard. Costs, recovery capacity and the risk of copying corruption still require a decision.

sections.heading: Practice · Assess protection and plan a restore
sections.body: Choose a fictional order or appointment dataset. Record its classification rationale, access rule, at-rest and in-transit safeguards, key owner and a residual risk. Explain what a hash can and cannot establish. Then write an exercise plan with explicit RTO/RPO, clock start/end, recovery-point measurement, isolated environment, restore owner, key/identity dependencies, integrity checks and a business acceptance transaction. Name the evidence and who decides what to do after a missed target. Complete the cross-week executive case using this assessment and your earlier risk, identity and architecture work. Keep resource consumption, task completion, card recall and rubric-based assessment separate.

The COO then examines a restore completed in 3h15m from a 90-minute-old recovery point: it meets the illustrative 4h RTO but misses the 1h RPO. The decision record assigns a follow-up exercise and retains both results.

payload.brief: Fictional Alder Supply accepts customer orders through a public portal and dispatches stock from managed warehouse terminals. The order API and inventory API use separate service identities but share an identity provider. A warehouse terminal can reach the backup console in the flat network. A contractor moved from support to reporting; its old local backup-admin role and a session remain active. A courier export contains delivery addresses. Disk encryption is enabled, but export handling and key recovery ownership are unclear. The COO sets a four-hour RTO and one-hour RPO for usable order-to-dispatch service. In an isolated synthetic exercise, disruption starts at 12:00, the usable point is 10:30, technical restore finishes 14:20, key permissions are fixed at 15:00 and business acceptance is 15:15. The next two-week pilot can change one management path and conduct one follow-up recovery test. No real incident frequency, financial loss or legal applicability is known.
payload.deliverable: Write a one-page executive decision note plus a flow/concept sketch. Include two risk chains, a joiner/mover/leaver access correction and user/admin/service safeguards, two flows and at least three boundaries, two controls with failure modes/tradeoffs, a classified-data assessment and a safe recovery plan. Evaluate both supplied recovery measurements, choose the pilot priority, name owners/evidence and state when to revisit. Use rubric-foundation-case@1 for criterion-level self-feedback; no automatic pass/readiness threshold is supplied.
constraints: Use only the invented facts; identify assumptions and missing evidence rather than inventing probabilities, law or employer details.
Do not connect to real systems, use real learner/employer artifacts or run destructive tests. Draw and describe synthetic allowed/denied checks.
Keep resource/task completion, card recall, question attempts and applied assessment distinct. This is self-assessment, not independent review or certification evidence.
State how the pilot preserves required dispatch work and handles emergency access; do not leave a universal bypass.
All teaching remains AI-authored draft pending independent educator review; unresolved source/claim concerns block validated publication.
payload.annotatedExample: Decision: pilot the restricted backup-management path and correct the contractor’s stale local role/session immediately through the accountable access owners; schedule the permitted follow-up recovery exercise. Chain 1: dispatch depends on orders; a compromised terminal reaches the console and reuses powerful access; reachable management plus stale privilege permits copy deletion; service recovery may fail (availability). Network owner restricts the path, backup owner removes obsolete privilege and tests allowed emergency administration; broad exception rules and approved-session misuse remain. Chain 2: delivery depends on address exports; a compromised clerk session uses excess export scope; unnecessary disclosure harms customers (confidentiality). Data/application owners restrict export scope and approved handling; authorised plaintext misuse remains. Identity: HR/contract trigger, service-owner approval, IAM execution and local-app verification govern joiners/movers/leavers; normal user access, time-limited separate admin access and scoped service credentials have different safeguards. Flows: customer browser → public entry → order API → order DB and managed terminal → internal entry → inventory API → stock DB; label entry, application and data boundaries with identity/permission decisions and owners. Neither flow grants backup administration. Protect the restricted fictional addresses at rest and in transit with named key custody and recovery; a bare digest without a trusted reference proves no origin. Recovery: 12:00 to 15:15 is 3h15m and meets the 4h RTO; 10:30 is 90 minutes before disruption and misses the 1h RPO. The recovery lead repeats an isolated synthetic restore with key/identity dependencies, timestamps, integrity reconciliation and an accepted order-to-dispatch transaction; database owner tests a newer recoverable point. Annotation: this is one defensible priority, not the single keyed response. Strong answers explicitly compare alternatives, state uncertainty and use each rubric criterion. One test does not prove all future recoveries or professional readiness.
